content: Brachial plexus injury (BPI) refers to damage to the brachial plexus, a network of nerves that extends from the spinal cord, specifically from the fifth cervical vertebra (C5) to the first thoracic vertebra (T1). This nerve network innervates and traverses the neck, axilla, and arm. BPI can lead to significant functional impairment in one or, in some cases, both upper limbs, resulting in an inability to perform daily activities. This can have profound consequences, including economic hardship, depression, and survival challenges in severe cases. The first documented case of obstetric brachial plexus injury was reported by Smellie in 1764. In 1872, Duchenne identified traction as a cause of BPI. Subsequently, Erb proposed that traction or pinching of the C5 or C6 nerve roots could also result in BPI. In 1900, Thourborn became the first scientist to publish an article on the direct repair of BPI components. By 1903, Harris and Low reported the first cases of neurotization. In 1920, Vulpian and Stoffel rerouted some fascicles of the pectoral nerves to the musculocutaneous and axillary nerves. In 1947, Seddon published his method for surgically correcting traction injuries using long interpositional nerve grafts. However, in 1966, during the Paris meeting of the International Society of Orthopedic Surgery and Traumatology (SICOT), it was concluded that surgical repair of BPI was nearly impossible. Later, Stevens provided a detailed explanation of the biomechanics of traction injuries in the upper limb and neck, as well as their impact on the brachial plexus. Pioneers such as Narakas, Millesi, Allieu, Brunelli, Gu, Terzis, Doi, and others successfully introduced microsurgical techniques for nerve repair and regeneration, advancing the field significantly.
